title: Setting up a night vision camera for lambing
subtitle: Monitor ewes overnight without disturbing the shed.
excerpt: A night vision camera in the lambing shed lets you check on ewes from the house without repeatedly walking out and disturbing the flock. A ewe close to lambing will show restlessness, pawing, and isolation from the group. Catching a difficult presentation early makes a significant difference to outcomes. Here is how to mount, connect, and use a night vision camera effectively.
sourceNotes: NSA (National Sheep Association), lambing management guidance. SAC Consulting, remote monitoring in sheep housing. NADIS, recognising signs of imminent lambing.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bank of infrared LEDs mounted on or near a night vision camera that flood an area with infrared light invisible to the naked eye. The camera sensor detects the reflected IR light, producing a clear monochrome image in total darkness.

content.text: A night vision camera works by illuminating the shed with

that sheep cannot detect. From the ewes' perspective the shed is completely dark. From the camera's perspective it is lit. The result is a clear, monochrome image of the entire pen on your phone without any disturbance to the flock.
Mount the camera at a height of 2 to 2.5 m, angled downward to cover the floor of the lambing pen. You need to see individual ewes lying down, not just moving around.
Position the camera so the feed rail, water trough, and any deep-bedded corners are all in frame. Ewes about to lamb often seek out a corner or the edge of the pen.
For a shed wider than 5 m, two cameras are more reliable than one. A single wide-angle camera may not give enough detail to read individual sheep at the far end.

Run a power cable to the camera (most farm night vision cameras run on 12V DC from a mains adapter). PoE (Power over Ethernet) cameras simplify installation: a single cable carries both power and data.
For wifi access from the house, a shed access point or a long-range wifi bridge is usually needed. Standard home wifi rarely reaches outbuildings reliably at 60 to 100 m.

Set the camera to record a clip when motion is detected, or to record continuously onto a local SD card or NVR. Motion-triggered clips on a phone let you see activity without watching a static feed all night.
What to watch for at lambing
A ewe pawing repeatedly at the bedding and getting up and down frequently: active first stage of labour.
A visible water bag or membrane at the vulva with no lamb presented after 30 minutes: attend immediately.
A ewe standing apart from the group with her head lowered: she may have just lambed or be in early labour. Check whether a lamb is present in the pen before going back to the house.
A lamb on its feet but not suckling after 20 minutes: mismothering risk, or the lamb cannot find the teat. Go out and assist.
